# The Shop for Unfinished Things

The clock in Mara’s window had been seven minutes slow for eleven years. People sometimes stopped to tell her, pointing through the glass with the satisfaction of someone who had noticed a loose button on a stranger’s coat. Mara thanked them and explained that the clock was not for sale. Its hands moved, its pendulum swung, and every Sunday it lost precisely seven minutes. Her husband had repaired it the week before he died, and she had never found the heart to correct his work.

The shop occupied a narrow brick building between a bakery and a vacant lot. Its sign read **REPAIRS**, though Mara repaired fewer things than she used to. Manufacturers had grown fond of sealed cases, special screws, and components that cost almost as much as the machines they inhabited. Still, people brought her lamps, radios, fans, and the occasional object they could not name. She kept a box under the counter for mysteries: pieces of metal and plastic whose owners had said, “It fell off, but everything seems to be working.”

On a wet Tuesday in March, a girl came in carrying a toaster wrapped in a blue towel. She was perhaps sixteen, with rain darkening the shoulders of her school uniform. She placed the bundle on the counter and explained that the toaster belonged to her grandmother. It had stopped working that morning, and her grandmother was convinced the house would burn down if anyone plugged it in again. The girl did not share this concern, but she did want toast.

Mara turned the toaster over. A crumb tray slid out, depositing a small brown dune on the counter. The girl watched closely as Mara removed the screws and lifted the casing.

“Do you know what you’re looking for?” she asked.

“Not yet,” Mara said. “First I’m looking at what’s there.”

A strip of bread had become wedged near the latch, keeping it from catching. Mara removed it with tweezers, brushed out the crumbs, and tested the mechanism. The toaster clicked down and stayed. She plugged it in briefly, watching the elements glow.

“How much?” the girl asked.

“Nothing this time. It took three minutes.”

The girl frowned. “You knew which three minutes.”

Her name was Leila, and she returned on Saturday with a desk lamp from her bedroom. The switch worked if held at a particular angle, which made reading difficult and occasionally alarming. Mara showed her how to unplug the lamp, open the base, and examine the connections. A wire had worked loose from its terminal. Leila tightened it herself, then put the lamp back together without being asked. When she finished, she stayed to help sort the screws that had accumulated in a biscuit tin.

By April, Leila came most weekends. She swept the floor, labelled drawers, and learned to tell Mara when she had no idea what she was doing. This was harder than learning the names of tools. Leila was quick and hated pausing in the middle of a task, especially when a customer was watching. Mara made her stop anyway. An hour spent reading a diagram, she said, could save a day spent explaining why someone’s grandfather’s radio was now two radios, neither of them functional.

Leila brought questions from school, too. She wanted to know why some materials conducted electricity and others didn’t, why rechargeable batteries eventually failed, and why Mara marked certain repairs in a red notebook. The notebook, Mara explained, was for jobs she had declined or mishandled. She recorded what had happened and what she might do differently. Leila flipped through it one afternoon and found pages of careful notes, including several labelled **COULD NOT FIX**.

“You kept all these?” she asked.

“They’re useful,” Mara said. “Besides, I remember them whether I write them down or not.”

At the end of April, a notice appeared on the shop door. The town council was considering a flood-control plan for the riverfront, including the block where the shop stood. Engineers had found that the existing embankment would not protect the lowest streets during a severe flood. One proposal called for a wider channel, a raised path, and the removal of fourteen buildings. The notice invited residents and business owners to a meeting at the library. It used the phrase *managed retreat*, which Mara read twice before folding the paper and putting it beneath the cash register.

The river had flooded before, though not badly in Mara’s lifetime. Every few years it climbed over the lower bank and filled the car park behind the grocery store. Children came to look at the water; adults moved their cars and compared the depth with previous years. Older residents talked about a flood decades earlier that had reached the railway tracks. There were photographs of it in the local history room, but the river had since been straightened and the banks reinforced. Most people treated those photographs as history.

Mara’s lease would expire in eighteen months. If the council approved the plan, the building’s owner could sell to the town, and the shop would have to move. Mara told herself she ought to be relieved. Her knees hurt when she stood for too long, the roof leaked near the back shelves, and she had been trying for three years to reduce her hours. Yet when she pictured the shop empty, she kept seeing the outlines left by everything she would remove: pale rectangles on the wall, screw holes, dustless patches beneath the cabinets.

Leila attended the meeting with her grandmother. Mara sat behind them, near the aisle. An engineer named Owen presented maps showing projected water levels under several scenarios. He spoke carefully about uncertainty: rainfall could vary, the timing of storms mattered, and no plan would eliminate every risk. The wider channel, he said, would give the river room to rise without forcing as much water into the streets. A woman from the council described compensation for property owners and a proposed relocation fund for businesses, though the amount available had not yet been settled.

During questions, a man from the bakery asked why the town could not simply build a higher wall. Owen said a wall was one option, but it would need to extend well beyond the affected block. It would also require pumps for rainwater trapped on the town side. The costs and maintenance would be substantial. Someone else asked whether the new channel would protect the houses downstream. Owen said the modelling suggested it would not worsen flooding there, but the town was commissioning a further review.

People left the meeting with different pieces of the presentation in mind. Some repeated the largest estimate of possible damage; others repeated the lowest. The bakery owner began a petition against demolition. A family living near the river put their house up for sale. At the hardware store, two men argued over whether the council had neglected the embankment or whether the plans were an excuse to redevelop the waterfront. Mara signed neither petition nor letter. She wanted to understand the decision, though she was beginning to suspect that understanding it would not make her like it.

In May, Leila brought an old portable radio into the shop. Its brown case was scuffed at the corners, and the handle had been replaced with a strip of leather. It had belonged to her grandfather, who had died when she was small. Her grandmother wanted to know whether it could receive the evening news again. Leila placed it on the bench with unusual care. She had few memories of her grandfather, but she remembered the radio on his kitchen table and the sound of him turning its dial.

The battery compartment was corroded. Mara showed Leila how to clean the contacts safely, and together they checked the wiring. A capacitor needed replacing, and the tuning cord had slipped from its track. They ordered the component and spent the following Saturday threading the cord around tiny wheels. Leila grew frustrated when it slipped for the fourth time. Mara suggested a break. They ate pastries on the back step, then returned to the bench and found that a spring had been hooked into the wrong hole.

When the radio finally worked, it produced a burst of static, followed by a man discussing the price of wheat. Leila laughed so loudly that a customer at the counter looked over. They turned the dial through music, traffic reports, and a station broadcasting in a language neither of them knew. The sound was thin and uneven, but it filled the room. Leila took a photograph for her grandmother, then stayed another hour to polish the case with a soft cloth.

The next week, her grandmother came by to thank Mara and brought an envelope of photographs. One showed the street outside the shop during the old flood. Water covered the pavement and reached halfway up a delivery van’s wheels. Another showed Leila’s grandfather standing on a ladder, passing boxes through an upstairs window. On the back he had written the date and the words **MOVED THE RECORDS JUST IN TIME**. Mara borrowed the photographs for the afternoon and walked them over to the library, where the history room kept a file on the flood.

The librarian found newspaper reports and a handwritten log kept by the fire station. The reports described evacuations, damaged roads, and volunteers carrying food to residents who could not leave their homes. The log listed calls with times and addresses, including several from the street where Mara’s shop now stood. It was useful evidence of what had happened, though it could not settle what might happen next. The riverbank was different now, as were the buildings and drainage systems. Mara made copies anyway, with the librarian’s permission, and brought them to Leila.

They spread the copies across the workbench after closing. Leila noticed that the fire station had recorded water entering the basement of the old printworks before anyone reported flooding on the road. The printworks had stood where the vacant lot was now. Mara found a note about a blocked drain two streets uphill. They began marking the addresses on a modern map, using different colours for road closures, flooded buildings, and rescue calls. By the time they stopped, the bakery next door had turned off its lights.

At the next council meeting, Mara brought the map. She did not offer it as proof that the proposed channel was necessary. Instead, she asked whether the engineers had used the fire station records and whether the blocked drains had been accounted for in the new modelling. Owen said he had seen some of the newspaper reports but not the complete log. He asked the librarian for copies and promised to pass the drainage question to the review team. Mara was glad she had spoken, even though her voice had shaken.

The council held two more meetings over the summer. The independent review supported the main findings but recommended changes to the downstream drainage plan. The proposed business relocation fund was increased after several owners described the cost of moving equipment and losing customers during a closure. The bakery owner still opposed demolition. So did Mara’s landlord, who submitted an alternative wall design for consideration. The engineers reviewed it and published a comparison. It would protect the block, they concluded, but would cost more over its expected life and leave less room for future changes to the river.

In August, the council voted to proceed with the channel. The work would be phased over several years, beginning downstream. Property purchases would take time, and the fourteen buildings would not all come down at once. There was applause from a few people in the chamber and angry shouting from others. Mara went home carrying a thick packet of documents. She put it on her kitchen table and left it there for a week, moving it aside each evening to make room for her plate.

Leila expected Mara to announce her retirement. Instead, one Saturday morning, Mara asked her to help measure the shop. They wrote down the dimensions of the benches, shelving, cabinets, and largest pieces of equipment. The measurements filled several sheets. Mara had seen a small unit for rent near the bus station, farther from the river. Its front window was plain, and the floor sloped slightly, but it had enough power outlets and a dry storeroom. She had not yet decided whether to take it.

They visited the unit together. Leila stood in the empty room, imagining the counter against one wall and the workbenches beneath the window. Mara checked the taps and looked closely at the ceiling. Outside, buses arrived and departed, bringing people from neighbourhoods that rarely passed the old shop. The rent was higher, but the relocation fund would cover some of the moving costs. After a week of calculations and an uncomfortable conversation with her accountant, Mara signed a lease beginning in January.

Word spread that the shop was moving. Customers came in to collect objects they had forgotten, including a hair dryer repaired eight months earlier and a brass lamp whose owner had moved away. Others brought new work, hoping to have it finished before the move. Mara began turning away large jobs she could not complete in time. Leila made a list of everything that needed packing and discovered, behind a cabinet, the missing back of a television that had left the shop years ago. They added it to the box of mysteries.

On the final afternoon, neighbours came to help carry the heavy benches into a rented van. The baker brought a tray of rolls; Leila’s grandmother wrapped the clock in old curtains. Mara walked through the rooms after everyone had gone outside. The shelves were bare, and the marks on the walls were just as she had imagined. She checked the cupboards, turned off the lights, and locked the door. Then she went back in because she had forgotten the red notebook on the windowsill.

The new shop opened three weeks later. On its first Saturday, a man arrived with a fan that rattled, followed by a woman carrying a kettle with a damaged handle. Leila took their names and wrote careful descriptions of the problems. Mara unwrapped the old clock and set it in the window, where it began its slow weekly drift. At closing time, Leila asked whether they should put up a notice explaining that it lost seven minutes.

“Let’s see how many people tell us first,” Mara said.

They locked the door and caught the bus home, leaving the clock swinging in the window.
